questions.q: What underlies Data Guard's primary/standby model, compared to a SQL Server FCI or classic Availability Group?
options: No shared quorum or Windows/Pacemaker cluster service — each standby is a complete, separate database kept current by redo transport and redo apply
Data Guard requires the exact same Windows Server Failover Clustering that SQL Server FCIs use
Data Guard requires shared storage between primary and standby, identical to an FCI
There is no meaningful difference at all between Data Guard and a Windows failover cluster
questions.explain: Data Guard's model is redo shipping and apply between independent databases, with no shared-quorum cluster resource manager underneath it.

questions.q: What is the difference between SYNC and ASYNC redo transport in Data Guard?
options: SYNC has the primary wait for standby confirmation before committing (zero data loss, more latency); ASYNC doesn't wait (less impact, small potential loss window)
SYNC and ASYNC are purely cosmetic settings with no functional difference
ASYNC guarantees zero data loss while SYNC allows data loss
SYNC only works for logical standbys and ASYNC only works for physical standbys
questions.explain: SYNC trades latency for zero data loss by waiting for standby confirmation; ASYNC trades a small potential data-loss window for lower primary impact.

questions.q: What is the key difference between Maximum Protection and Maximum Availability protection modes?
options: Both guarantee zero data loss via synchronous transport, but Maximum Protection shuts the primary down if no standby can confirm, while Maximum Availability keeps the primary running
Maximum Availability guarantees zero data loss while Maximum Protection allows data loss
Maximum Protection is the default mode, and Maximum Availability must be purchased separately
There is no difference — they are two names for the same mode
questions.explain: Both use synchronous transport for zero data loss, but they differ in what happens if the standby becomes unreachable: shut down (Maximum Protection) vs. keep running (Maximum Availability).

questions.q: What distinguishes a switchover from a failover in Data Guard?
options: A switchover is a planned, no-data-loss role swap where both databases end up healthy; a failover is an unplanned promotion after the primary is actually lost
A switchover always causes data loss, while a failover never does
They are identical operations, just triggered by different commands
A switchover can only be performed by the Fast-Start Failover Observer
questions.explain: Switchover is a deliberate, clean role reversal for maintenance or testing; failover is a forced promotion when the primary is genuinely unavailable.

questions.q: What does Fast-Start Failover add to a standard Data Guard configuration?
options: An opt-in Observer process that can trigger automatic failover without a DBA manually initiating it
It is the default, always-on behavior of every Data Guard configuration
It removes the need for redo transport entirely
It converts every standby into a primary simultaneously
questions.explain: Fast-Start Failover is an opt-in feature where an Observer process monitors primary and standby health and can trigger an automatic failover, unlike default Data Guard behavior which requires manual action.
